standard.title: Citizenship and political change
standard.description: changes in Australia's political system and to Australian citizenship after Federation and throughout the 20th century that impacted First Nations Australians, migrants, women and children
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students understand the key values and features of Australian democracy. From AC9HS6K01 (Federation and democracy): Students have just studied the founding of Australia's democratic system.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the changes in Australia's political system and citizenship that impacted First Nations Australians, migrants, women and children after Federation and throughout the 20th century, assessing the significance of key changes.

nodes.label: First Nations Australians and political rights
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the significance of the 1962 right to vote federally and the 1967 referendum for First Nations Australians, and explain what these changes meant for citizenship and political recognition.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what happened in 1962 and 1967 for First Nations Australians and why these events were significant.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the significance of the 1962 right to vote federally and the importance of the 1967 referendum for First Nations Australians — what changed, what had been in place before, and why these changes mattered for citizenship, political recognition and the relationship between First Nations peoples and the Australian state.
wider: Investigate the campaign for the 1967 referendum — who organised it, what arguments were made, and how the Yes vote result was achieved
Explore the ongoing campaign for constitutional recognition of First Nations Australians, and assess what further changes advocates argue are still needed
nodes.hinge_reason: The exclusion and then inclusion of First Nations Australians in civic and political life is foundational to understanding Australia's democratic history — students who treat democracy as having always been inclusive will misunderstand both the struggles that created change and the significance of what was achieved.

response_modes.reason: Use a before/after framework to make the political exclusion visible before the change — students need to understand what the situation was before 1962 and 1967 to appreciate the significance of the change.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The campaign for the 1967 referendum is a rich and historically significant case study in civic action. It connects to AC9HS5K07 (citizens working for civic goals) and offers important depth in understanding how democratic change happens.
success_criteria: Students explain what changed for First Nations Australians in 1962 and 1967.
Students describe why these changes were significant for citizenship and political recognition.

nodes.label: Women and the advance of democracy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain key developments in advancing democracy and citizenship for women in Australia across the 20th century, including the suffragette movement, right to vote, equal pay and anti-discrimination legislation.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two developments that advanced the rights of women in Australia and explain why each was significant.
nodes.typical_width: Explain key developments in advancing democracy for women: the suffragette movement and winning the right to vote, the bar on married women working in the public service, the equal pay campaign, and the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 — placing each in chronological context and explaining its significance.
wider: Investigate the life and contribution of a specific figure in the Australian women's rights movement and explain their role in achieving a particular change
Compare the pace and nature of democratic change for women in Australia with that in another country, and assess what factors influenced the timing and form of change

response_modes.reason: The timeline of change for women spans the full 20th century — students benefit from placing individual developments in chronological sequence to understand that democratic inclusion was a long, contested process.

success_criteria: Students describe at least two developments that advanced democratic rights for women.
Students place each development in approximate chronological context and explain its significance.

nodes.label: Migrants, children and expanding citizenship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain changes to citizenship and democratic participation for migrants and children in Australia across the 20th century, including the minimum wage, anti-discrimination legislation and multicultural policy.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two changes that expanded democratic rights or citizenship for migrants or children.
nodes.typical_width: Explain key developments advancing democracy for all citizens, including migrant groups: establishment of the minimum wage, anti-discrimination legislation, official multicultural policy — and for children: experiences in orphanages and homes, protections introduced over time.
wider: Investigate the experience of a specific migrant group in Australia during the 20th century and assess how legislation and policy affected their citizenship rights
Explore the history of child welfare legislation in Australia, including the Stolen Generations, and evaluate the long-term impacts on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities

response_modes.reason: The range of groups whose citizenship expanded across the 20th century is the key breadth dimension — students benefit from comparison across groups to see democratic change as a broad social process rather than isolated events.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Stolen Generations and child welfare legislation is a significant and historically important direction connecting to First Nations Australian history, reconciliation, and ongoing policy debates with contemporary relevance.
success_criteria: Students describe at least two changes that expanded citizenship rights for migrants or children.
Students explain the significance of each change for the groups affected.

nodes.label: Democracy as an evolving system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that Australia's political system and citizenship have changed significantly since Federation, assessing the significance of key changes for different groups and describing the nature of democracy as an evolving rather than fixed system.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two changes to Australia's democratic system or citizenship since Federation and assess the significance of each for the group most affected.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the range of changes to Australia's democratic system and citizenship since Federation for First Nations Australians, women, migrants and children; assess the significance of each change; describe how these changes reflect democracy as a system that evolves in response to social movements and changing values.
wider: Evaluate which change to Australian citizenship or the political system since Federation was most significant overall, constructing and defending an argument with evidence
Assess what further changes to Australian democracy might be needed today, drawing on the pattern of 20th century change as a guide to what remains unfinished

response_modes.reason: The integration challenge is moving from a series of individual changes to a coherent understanding of democratic evolution. Support students to identify the pattern across cases — that democratic inclusion has expanded over time through advocacy and legislation.

success_criteria: Students explain changes to Australia's democratic system for at least two different groups.
Students assess the significance of at least one change for the group affected.
Students describe democracy as an evolving system rather than a fixed one.
